6.140.m: The venerable Mahādeva said: / O goddess, I shall speak of another, the great confluence of the Hiraṇyā, / when the Sābhramatī Gaṅgā became seven streams in ancient times.
Then that daughter of Brahmā was celebrated as "having seven streams"; / the seventh is called the stream named Hiraṇyā.
A person, even a sinner, having bathed in that sacred place, attains the highest destiny. / Between the Ṛkṣu and the Mañju lies the mountain named Satyavat.
To the east of it is the auspicious, very great sacred place, the confluence of the Hiraṇyā; / having bathed and sipped water there, one attains an auspicious destiny.
Then one should go to the forest site, having seen Nārāyaṇa Hari, / the holy sacred place of the celestial nymphs, Hiraṇyāsaṃgameśvara,
where Urvaśī, the auspicious one among all celestial nymphs, was born in ancient times; / Nara and Nārāyaṇa performed supreme asceticism there,
at the delightful, auspicious confluence of the Hiraṇyā which removes great sins, / where all the sages, freed from impurities, indeed bathe.
The brāhmaṇas beginning with Vasiṣṭha, and those beginning with the Vālakhilyas, / bathe, O sovereign of the gods, at the confluence with the Hiraṇyā.
Where a golden form is surely obtained from bathing; / whatever fruit comes from the gift of a thousand brown cows,
that fruit one always obtains at the confluence of the Hiraṇyā. / Whatever religious merit [is gained] at ten horse sacrifices, or during an eclipse of the moon and sun,
that is proclaimed to be multiplied infinitely at the confluence of the Hiraṇyā. / And whatever fruit one may obtain from the gift of one's weight in gold,
that fruit one always obtains at the confluence of the Hiraṇyā. / The great Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa performed great asceticism there;
his body became gold-like there in ancient times. / Likewise, when King Janamejaya bathed there,
the sin of killing a brāhmaṇa departed, O goddess, at the confluence of the Hiraṇyā. / Then the royal sage Viśvāmitra arrived for the purpose of bathing;
having taken a bath particularly [well], he went to my own city.
Brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and also śūdras, O goddess of gods, / who take a bath here go to Śiva's abode.

6.141.m: Mahādeva said: / Then, O goddess, I shall speak after the confluence of the Hiraṇyā, / where the river Dharmāvatī joins with the Gaṅgā.
A blessed man, having bathed there, goes to heaven without doubt; / whoever sees the sacred place made by Dharma shares in religious merit.
Those who perform an ancestral offering right there are released from debt to the ancestors. / And next is Madhurātīrtha, destroying all sins;
one should bathe in Madhurātīrtha, and Hari, the slayer of Madhu, should be seen, / where Kṛṣṇa, distressed by fear of Jarāsandha, rested,
after the slaying of the demon Kaṃsa had occurred, desiring to go to Kuśasthalī. / Having stayed for seven nights on the bank of the Candanā,
surrounded by the Bhojas, Vṛṣṇis, and Andhakas, the heroic bulls of the Yādavas, / having reached Madhurātīrtha and bathed according to the proper rite,
where Hari established the one named Madhurāditya; / having settled eighteen thousand brāhmaṇas rich in sacrifices,
and having given various conveyances, he departed. / And thousands of sacred places reside there, O goddess of gods;
an ancestral offering should be performed there with the desire for the ancestors' benefit: / "No fear should be felt of Jarāsandha by those always dwelling in my sacred place."
Having spoken thus to those twice-born, Kṛṣṇa departed toward Dvārakā. / Having bathed at that ford, a man should worship Madhurārka.
by donating a brown cow on the bright seventh of Māgha, / he enjoys pleasures for a long time here, and goes to the realm of the sun.
Listen, O beautiful woman, I shall tell an ancient history, / hearing which a person is released from sins such as the killing of a brāhmaṇa.
At one time, O goddess, the excellent sage Māṇḍavya / performed great, highly meritorious asceticism at Gaṅgādvāra,
eating leaves, eating fruit, and always consuming air; / day and night, O goddess, always devoted to the meditation on Viṣṇu,
ever delighting in the practice of yoga, ever devoted to righteousness. / In that country, O goddess, there was a king, Viśvamohana;
he possessed abundant wealth of elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers on the earth. / His son, famous as Somacandra, possessed auspicious marks.
Once upon a time, O goddess, he went into the forest on a hunt; / having gone there at that time, having performed the acts of the hunt,
he amused himself, surrounded by his own people. / While the king was engaged in sporting, O goddess of gods, night fell.
During that night, the king stayed in the hunting forest. / When that night had passed, at the moment called the hour of Brahmā,
a horse was specially stolen there by an evil-minded thief. / Then an outcry arose: "Where did the horse go? Where did it go?"
Then, out of fear of the king, all were anxious and eager to go, / saying indeed: "The horse was carried away by a thief!"
Searching all around, they all came to Haridvāra; / there, indeed, the sage Māṇḍavya was constantly performing asceticism,
and absorbed in meditation, he was seen by those soldiers then: / "This thief, always a sinner, remains absorbed in meditation!
He came here after tying up the horse!"—so it was considered by the royal soldiers then. / Thinking thus, all of them seized that great sage,
and presented that excellent sage as a thief to the king: / "The horse-stealer has been brought; this thief always [acts thus], O king!"
Then an order was given by him for impaling on a stake; / then, having gathered together, all those soldiers bound him.
Afterwards, he was impaled on a stake from that very moment; / that act of piercing by the stake was not known by him,
because he was absorbed in yoga, devoted to the meditation on Viṣṇu. / After some time had passed, the impalement on the stake was perceived [by him]:
"I am Māṇḍavya, the best of sages; by whom was this act done?" / The lord, omniscient and knowing the three divisions of time, reflected on it:
"This is the deed of Dharma, and never of anyone else." / That righteous one, absorbed in yoga, went to the presence of Dharma.
Having gone there, he said this: "Listen now, O Dharma! / You are indeed celebrated as Dharma in the world and in the Veda at all times;"
"Why was the deed of impalement upon a stake done by you? / I wish to hear all that from you, O god; there is no doubt."
Dharma said: / "Listen, O best of twice-born, to the sin in your previous birth. / I shall tell you that; have mercy upon me.
This deed was a sin committed in your previous birth during your childhood. / Listen to that, O very wise one, because of which this falling was brought about in this life.
At one time, O vipra, you went into a solitary forest. / Having gone there, O vipra, a living creature called a grasshopper
was indeed impaled upon a thorn by you, afflicted by that deed. / You were indeed placed upon a stake by the king because of this deed, O you of good vows.
The deed done, good or bad, must by all means be experienced. / This was merely a small deed experienced by you; there is no doubt.
May you be happy, O lord of vipras; go as you wish." / Hearing this speech, then, Māṇḍavya, best of the twice-born,
spoke words there, his eyes fierce with anger: / Māṇḍavya said: / "Hey, most sinful, wicked-minded one, why was so great a sin caused,
on account of which this deed of impalement on a stake was done? / By the fury of my curse, you shall by all means become a śūdra!"
In the course of some time, in the lunar lineage, / he was born by the name of Vidura, devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu.
Under the pretext of a pilgrimage, he went to the Sābhramatī River, / where the confluence with the Dharmāvatī exists, O goddess of the gods.
There indeed Vidura, the embodiment of dharma, took a bath; / there his śūdra status was abandoned in the Dharmāvatī; there is no doubt.
For this reason, O goddess, wherever men take a bath [there], / those men of meritorious deeds go to the supreme abode.

Those men on earth who perform a śrāddha and give gifts here, / having obtained supreme prosperity in this world, rejoice in heaven.

Thus in the glorious Padma Purāṇa, in the collection of fifty-five thousand verses, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara, in the glorification of the Sābharmatī, the glorification of Madhurāditya,

6.142.m: The glorious Mahādeva said: / A man, having bathed in Kaṃbutīrtha or having offered libations to the ancestors, / should worship the lord of the gods, the disease-free Nārāyaṇa.
Having given gifts duly to the brāhmaṇas according to the precept, / he attains the world of Viṣṇu by the power of this tīrtha.
Here, in the past, by the wise royal sage Viśvāmitra / austere asceticism was performed especially, desiring offspring, O beautiful woman.
Where he lived subsisting on wind, taking no food, eating only air, / constantly devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, intent on meditating upon Viṣṇu.
Through this asceticism, he became one who obtained his desire for offspring. / And whatever man desiring offspring goes to Kaṃbutīrtha,
he constantly obtains offspring; it is true, it is true, O fair-faced woman!
Thus ends the glorification of the Kaṃbu Ford. / Then one should go, O best of gods, to the ford named Kapīśvara, / in the presence of the red lion, which destroys great sins.
Formerly, when the bridge was being built during the war between Rāma and Rāvaṇa, / taking the best of mountains, it was constructed particularly by the monkeys.
They established the unsurpassed tīrtha named Kapīśvarāditya. / Where, after bathing in the tīrtha or offering libations to the ancestors,
having seen Kapīśvarāditya, one is freed from the murder of a brāhmaṇa. / A bath should be taken there especially on the eighth day of Caitra,
where a bath was taken for three days by those headed by Hanumat. / This power of Kapitīrtha has been related to you.
Having bathed in this tīrtha and having worshipped Kapīśvara, a man / becomes handsome and endowed with many enjoyments; there is no doubt here.
Whatever person desires strength, or dharma, or a son, / he always obtains all that by the power of Kapitīrtha.

6.143.m: Then one should go to Ekadhāra, the supremely purifying tīrtha. / Having bathed at Ekadhāra, fasting for one night,
worshipping the lord of the gods, the Master, he can save a hundred families. / The immersion in this tīrtha is to be known as equal to Svāmitīrtha.
A man would go to the world of Rudra by the power of this tīrtha; / and having bathed and drunk there, he also goes to the world of Brahmā.
Those of meritorious deeds in the three worlds reside indeed upon this bank.
They have no fear, and whatever [fear of] sword's edges and the like exists, / all that is quickly destroyed at this chief Ekadhāra tīrtha.
Thus ends the description of the Ekadhāra Ford. / Then one should go to Saptadhāra, the supreme of sacred fords, / named Saptasārasvata, which was formed by the sages for its sake.
In the Tretā age, Maṅkitīrtha was made by the great sage Maṅki; / but in the Dvāpara age, Saptadhāra was established by the sons of Pāṇḍu.
The tīrtha fallen from Hara's matted locks attained the state of having seven streams. / The seven forms of the Gaṅgā that flow in the seven worlds,
those sacred waters flow in this Saptadhāra tīrtha. / A śrāddha performed at Saptadhāra grants satisfaction to the ancestors.
Listen, O goddess, I shall proclaim an ancient legendary history, / hearing which, O goddess of the lords of gods, one will surely go to the world of Brahmā.
There was a son of Kauṣītaka, known indeed by the name of Maṅki, / constantly delighting in meditating on Viṣṇu, worshipping the world of Viṣṇu,
a reciter of the Vedas, and devoted to the agnihotra. / In his house were two wives: Surūpā and Viśvarūpā.
Seeing them devoid of sons, O goddess, he became apprehensive. / Pondering 'What is to be done?', he became filled with immense anxiety:
"A lineage becomes firm only through a son; otherwise one goes to hell." / Thus brooding with anxiety, he found no happiness anywhere.
Then, having left his home, he went into the presence of his guru: / "Salutation indeed to you, O guru, benefactor of the gods!
You are the protector of all worlds and the preserver of the brāhmaṇas. / You are the performer of sacrifices, O king of the twice-born; obeisance to you.
I am sonless, O sage among vipras; what is to be done, O lord? / Speak in such a manner that a son will certainly be born.
For a sonless man there is no destination in heaven, none at all; / by whatever means possible, one should bring about the birth of a son."
"Remembering this statement, I have come into your presence."
The guru said: / "Go, O tiger among sages, where the Sābhramatī River is; / having gone there, O best of sages, you will surely obtain sons."
Having heard that statement of his and bowed like a stick, / that king among vipras went toward the Sābhramatī River.
The sage among vipras named Maṅki, having gone there, / then performed great asceticism, O goddess, for a period of four years.
Where a tīrtha was established by that Maṅki who spoke the Veda, / in the Tretā age then, O goddess, that tīrtha of great wonder
arose there, without doubt, bestowing sons and granting all desires. / Even today, there has never been nor will there be anything equal to Maṅkitīrtha.
Having obtained sons as he wished and enjoyed diverse pleasures, / that best of twice-borns, Maṅki, went to my abode.

6.143.m:
This divine narrative is supreme, purifying, and great; / merely by hearing it, one attains happiness through sons and everything else.

Then one should go, O goddess of the gods, to Brahmavallī, a great ford. / Listen directly to the nature of that ford, O best of the gods.

Where the water of the Sābhramatī unites with the water of the Brahmavallī, / that Brahmatīrtha is considered equal to Prayāga.

By offering a rice-ball there, the ancestors certainly attain satisfaction / for twelve years, in accordance with the word of Brahmā.

The merit at Brahmavallī is especially equal to a śrāddha at Gayā; / performing it there consciously, the ancestors find satisfaction.

The gift of a cow, the gift of land, and likewise the gift of food— / the merit [obtained] especially at Brahmavallī is equal to these gifts.

Right here, Sanaka and the others, having bathed according to the rules, / reached the world of Viṣṇu through meditation on the supreme state of Brahman.

Whatever fruit a man obtains by going to Puṣkara, / to the Gaṅgā, and to the sacred field of Amarakaṇṭaka, O ruler of the gods,

that very fruit he fully attains especially at Brahmavallī. / And whatever gift men give during an eclipse of the moon or the sun,

Thus ends the glorification of the Brahmavallī Ford. / Then one should go to the Vṛṣa Ford, renowned in Khaṇḍatīrtha, / where, having bathed in ancient times, cows attained heaven and Goloka.

Because cows, the mothers of the world, fallen through a curse, were rescued / by Dharma in the form of a bull, it is therefore called Khaṇḍatīrtha.

Pārvatī said: / Whose curse, indeed, fell upon the cows, the mothers of the worlds, in the past? / How did they fall from their world, and how were they protected by Dharma?

Mahādeva said: / Formerly in Goloka, as a bull was sporting with the cows, / dung and urine were dropped and fell upon the head of Hara.

Then Hara gave them a curse on account of that fault: / 'Deprived of consciousness, cows, you shall depart from your own world to the earth!'

Cursed by the Lord, the cows propitiated Hara again, / and begged the god: 'May we regain our world!'

6.143.m:
[Hara said:] 'When you bathe in the pool named Khaṇḍa, / near the Brahmavallī at the Sābhramatī sacred bath, you shall surely attain heaven.'

Then, having bathed in that pool along with the bull, / the cows, exceedingly purified, went to heaven into the presence of Mahādeva.

Having bathed in the Cow Pool and performed the water offering to the ancestors, / a person attains the world of the cows, free from burning and dissolution.

Remaining there without food, if one gives a rice-ball for cows, / that person thrives in happiness for as long as the fourteen Indras reign.

Whatever fruit is surely obtained by the donation of ten million cows, / that fruit one completely attains at Khaṇḍatīrtha, without a doubt.

The person who takes bull's urine and drinks that holy water / is instantly purified at Khaṇḍatīrtha, without a doubt.

There was never, nor will there ever be, a sacred place superior to Khaṇḍatīrtha. / Those men who go there, O best of goddesses, share in great merit.

Having gone there, O best of goddesses, one should worship cows; / then, having worshipped the bull, one should bathe with a composed mind.

Through that worship, without a doubt, one will dwell in Goloka for a long time. / Those who, having gone there, especially give a golden cow,
those men enjoy happiness for as long as the fourteen Indras reign. / Whoever then prepares and gives ten cows to a twice-born person
at Khaṇḍatīrtha, O best of goddesses, that is considered to yield infinite fruit. / Having gone there, the wise should plant a peepal tree.
When that is done, O ruler of the gods, he goes to the world of the ancestors. / Those who plant five divine myrobalan trees,
having enjoyed happiness in this world, go to the realm of Hari.

6.145.m: The glorious Mahādeva said: / Then one should go to the excellent, great sacred place Saṅgameśvara, / where the holy Hastimatī meets the Sābhramatī.
Having received a curse from the sage Kauṇḍinya, the river dried up, / and it became famous in the world under the name Bahiscarī.
I shall describe that holy place, renowned in the three worlds, / which removes all sins, is sacred, and is celebrated in the three worlds.
A man who bathes in that sacred place and beholds the god Maheśvara / is freed from all sins and goes to the world of Rudra.
Listen, O goddess, I shall explain the cause of this curse, / how she became dried up here on account of the curse.
Where the holy Sābhramatī, a great river named Gaṅgā, flows, / there the river named Hastimatī is joined with that Gaṅgā.
There, a sage undertook an exceedingly great ascetic penance; / thus, after much time had passed for that sage of noble soul,
Hṛṣīkeśa, the taintless Nārāyaṇa, was worshipped [by him]. / On her bank, O ruler of the gods, many years
passed for that sage, O Pārvatī. / One day, by the turn of fate, the rainy season arrived.
The river then became completely flooded through the arrival of the season, O faithful one; / then, in the night, the sage Kauṇḍinya had to abandon his hermitage.
At night, great sorrow arose; weeping pitiably, 'Alas, alas!', / he was overcome with intense anxiety, wondering, 'What should be done?'
For his great divine hermitage, together with the sage himself, / was carried away by the rush of water into the Hastimatī, O best of goddesses.
Fruits, roots, and many books— / they all were swept away in her by the rush of water, O beautiful one.
That Kauṇḍinya, best of sages, cursed that river indeed: / 'You shall become devoid of water in the Kali age!'
Having thus pronounced a curse upon the Hastimatī, O great goddess, / that best among Brahmins departed to the eternal world of Viṣṇu.
Even today that sacred place known as Saṅgameśvara exists; / seeing it, even a sinner is freed from the sin of Brahmin-murder and the like.

6.146.m: Mahādeva said: / Then one should go, O ruler of the gods, to the sacred place Rudramahālaya, / matchless like Kedāra, created directly by Rudra.
Right there, a śrāddha should be performed for the satisfaction of the ancestors; / through offering a śrāddha there, the fathers together with the grandfathers [attain satisfaction].
Satisfied, they go to the supreme abode of Rudra. / And whoever releases a bull there at Rudramahālaya,
either on the full moon of Kārttika or on that of Vaiśākha, rejoices with Rudra. / Having drunk water at Kedāra, rebirth is no more.
Here, merely by bathing, one shares in liberation, without a doubt. / Once, O goddess, having left Kailāsa, I arrived [here],
recognising the Sābhramatī as the great Gaṅgā, truly for the welfare of the world. / Having bathed there, and drunk, and made it an unsurpassed holy ford,
I then returned to my own abode, to Kailāsa, O passionate lady. / After that, the greatly meritorious holy ford Mahālaya came into being.

It will attain fame in the world as Rudramahālaya. / Those who go there on the full moon of Kārttika or of Vaiśākha, O best among the gods, / have no sorrow whatsoever born of worldly existence again.

6.147.m: Mahādeva said: / O goddess, listen now to the holy ford rare even for the gods, / known as Khaṅgatīrtha, which destroys all sins.
A person having bathed at Khaṅgatīrtha and seen Śiva Khaṅgeśvara / does not go to a bad destiny; he goes to the heavenly world.
Whoever beholds the god Khaṅgadhāreśvara, O best among the gods, / and especially arranges worship there on the full moon of Kārttika—
this god Viśveśvara on earth, O beloved, always / gives everything; the lord of all grants desired ends.
He who desires kingdom and wealth, and beholds that Lord in the month of Vaiśākha, / obtains that goal swiftly by the grace of Viśvanātha.
Then with flowers, incense, food offerings, or lamps, O daughter of the mountain, / and with gifts of fruits and bilva leaves, one should worship the lord of the universe.
He grants wealth and grain, and quickly confers the fortunes of sons, grandsons, and so forth; / there is no doubt that these are obtained from worship of glorious Viśveśvara.

6.148.m: Mahādeva said: / On the bank of the Sābhramatī is an unsurpassed holy ford, the Gayā ford, / auspicious, named Citrāṅgavadana, presided over by Mālārka,
adorned with groves of wish-fulfilling trees and mandāra flowers, / and with mango, neem, kadamba, kāśmarya, aśvattha, and tinduka trees.
It takes away leprosy from him, even through confusion of memory over a league; / for anyone who develops leprosy, Mālārka removes it.
Any woman who bathes there according to the Vedic injunctions, / whether her children have died or she is barren, soon obtains a son.
Twilight devotions, bathing, recitation, oblation, private Vedic study, and worship of the deities / performed by a devotee of the sun at Mālārka become imperishable.
Having gone there, O ruler of the gods, one should observe the vow of the glorious Sun; / having enjoyed happiness in this world, he indeed goes to the realm of the Sun.
A royal sage whose children had died went there and practiced penance; / that king obtained a son by the grace of the glorious Mālārka.
Having gone there, fasting especially, with senses subdued, / whoever worships Mālārka surely becomes a sharer in liberation.
The brāhmaṇas headed by Vasiṣṭha and the gods beginning with Indra constantly / dwell, O best of the gods, at Mālārka in the presence of the Sun.

6.149.m: Mahādeva said: / Beyond that holy ford is another holy ford situated within Mālārka; / one should go to Candaneśvara, an excellent place of delight.
Having drunk the blood of Duḥśāsana, the mighty Bhīma, / having fulfilled his entire dread vow,
and having bound up Draupadī's hair with hands smeared with blood, / made gifts to the twice-born and then set out on a pilgrimage to holy fords.
He went with his brothers to the charming bank of the Sābhramatī, / where a sandalwood tree had been brought down from heaven to the Sābhramatī.
By the power of that holy ford, it turned into the form of a liṅga. / Having bathed there, and drunk, and performed the libation to the ancestors,
a man would not go to hell; he would attain the realm of Rudra. / Then, beholding Candaneśa, the lord of the universe who brings auspiciousness to the world,
one should worship him to the best of one's ability, [reaching that place] having gone whereto one does not grieve. / Where a fisherman king, having performed worship many times,
went to that realm of Śiva, having reached which one does not grieve; / where the sages bathe, where the eternal god,
the Supreme Self Viṣṇu in visible form, always resides, granting prosperity. / Fortunate is this Sābhramatī; fortunate is the sovereign Lord of the Universe,
where many holy fords have come into existence on earth, O Pārvatī. / And here, with holy āmalakī fruits and auspicious fruits of various kinds,
an offering of water should be made according to rule, O beautiful lady.

6.150.m: Mahādeva said: / Then one should go for a bath to Jambūtīrtha, which destroys sins, / which stands like a stairway to heaven for men in the Kali age;
where formerly, upon Daśāṅga, the best of mountains, Jāmbavat / installed the liṅga of Ṛkṣarājeśa, worshipped by the host of gods.
When of old the demon Rāvaṇa was slain by Rāma, / then Jāmbavat proclaimed aloud in all directions with the sounds of kettledrums:
"Victory has been won by Rāmacandra! Rāvaṇa is slain in battle! / Sītā is recovered!" So proclaiming, he bathed at that auspicious, best of holy fords,
and established a liṅga there in his own name, O ruler of the gods. / Having bathed there, a man who immediately remembers Rāma along with his younger brother,

and having bathed at Jāmbavanteśvara, is honored in the realm of Rudra. / Wherever, O goddess, remembrance of glorious Rāma is made, / release from the bonds of worldly existence is indeed seen among mobile and immobile beings.
I should be known as Rāma, and Rāma is Rudra himself; / knowing thus, O goddess, no difference exists anywhere.
Those who mentally recite 'Rāma, Rāma, Rāma' / will obtain the attainment of all their aims in age after age.
I myself always, O goddess, practice remembrance of glorious Rāma, / hearing which, O goddess, worldly existence never occurs again.
Constantly residing in Kāśī, I continuously remember lotus-eyed glorious Rāma / with devotion according to the prescribed rules, O goddess.
Then, having of old remembered handsome Rāma, Jāmbavat / installed [the liṅga] known as Jāmbavanta, the guru of the worlds.
Having bathed and eaten there, and performed worship of the god, / one attains the realm of Śiva for as long as fourteen Indras reign.
Merely by bathing here, just as Jāmbavat had strength, / in the same way one obtains strength through the grace of the glorious Lord of the Universe.
And whatever man goes there and makes a gift of land, / his fruit is multiplied a thousandfold from seeing Jāmbavanteśa.

6.151.m: Mahādeva said: / Beyond this tīrtha is another tīrtha known as Indragrāma, / where in ancient times Śakra bathed and was freed from dreadful sin.
Pārvatī said: / By what deed here did Śakra incur dreadful sin, / and how did he become free of sin? Speak this at length.
Mahādeva said: / Formerly, Indra, the lord of the gods, and Namuci, the lord of the asuras, / made a mutual pact of slaying without weapons.
Then Indra, by the instruction of a voice from the sky, / took up foam and slew Namuci; then the murder of a brāhmaṇa occurred.
And Śakra asked his guru about the means to destroy the sin. / Then, by Bṛhaspati's instruction, on the northern bank of the Sābhramatī,
the lord of the gods arrived at this place and made his abode. / Merely by his bathing here, his sin immediately vanished,
and a luster as white as the full moon arose upon his body. / The slayer of Vṛtra installed the Lord as Dhavaleśvara.
And that linga became famous on the surface of the earth under Indra's name. / On the full moon day, and on the new moon day, at a solstice, and during an eclipse,
when a śrāddha is performed, there is twelve years' satisfaction for the ancestors. / Whoever approaches Dhavaleśvara and feeds brāhmaṇas,
when one brāhmaṇa is fed, a thousand are fed. / Gold, land, and garments should be given according to one's capacity;
a white cow with a calf and giving milk should be given to a brāhmaṇa. / Whatever brāhmaṇa comes here and performs the recitation of the Rudra hymn and other rites,
what is done by him is multiplied ten-millionfold by the grace of glorious Maheśa. / Whatever man undertakes fasting and other observances at this tīrtha,
he indeed becomes rich in all desires; there is no doubt. / Bringing a bilva leaf, whoever worships that Lord
obtains dharma, wealth, and pleasure as a human on earth. / Those best of men who go there especially on a Monday,
Dhavaleśvara pacifies their disease and fault. / Or when one performs worship especially on a Sunday,
their greatness, O goddess, has never been fully known by me. / Those who perform worship here with dūrvā grass, arka flowers,
white water-lilies, and lotus petals, those men partake of merit. / Bringing white arka flowers and worshiping Dhavaleśa,
one constantly attains what is desired, by the grace of Dhavaleśa. / In the Kṛta age he is Nīlakaṇṭha, always Śaṅkara to all;
in the Tretā age he is renowned as Hara, the blessed Lord; / in the Dvāpara age his name is Śarva, and in the Kali age he is Dhavaleśvara.
Hear what happened in ancient times in this regard, O ruler of the gods! / Formerly a vaiśya named Nandin dwelt in Indragrāma.
Intent on meditation upon Śiva, he performed the worship of Śiva. / He constantly worshiped the liṅga named Dhavala, situated in the penance grove.
Rising at every dawn, that beloved of Śiva, Nandin, / was exceedingly devoted every day to the worship of the liṅga.
He was intent on worshiping with flowers according to the scriptural rule. / Once, a violent hunter, eager for the chase,
a sinner of sinful conduct, roaming on the bank of the Sābhramatī / crowded with many beasts of prey, striking down deer with arrows,
wandering thus, that violent hunter / came by chance to the place where the well-worshiped liṅga stood,
renowned as Dhavaleśvara, adorned with many wonders. / He saw the well-worshiped liṅga with various flowers and fruits.
Having thus approached the liṅga, he went to the bank of the Sābhramatī. / Drinking water there, he then filled his mouth with a mouthful [of water],
and holding deer meat in one hand, / while bearing bilva leaves with the other hand for the sake of worship,
he quickly came near the liṅga and kicked away the worship with his foot. / All those flowers were scattered here and there.
The bathing of that liṅga was performed with the water from his mouthful. / With one hand he offered bilva leaves for worship,
and with the second hand he offered the deer meat. / Prostrating like a staff, he formed a resolve in his mind:
'From this day forward I will diligently perform worship. / You are my master and I am your devotee from this day forward, O Śaṅkara.'
Having thus taken a vow, the hunter went home. / Then at dawn, [Nandin] came to the temple of the god.
Nandin saw all that had been done by the hunter, / and seeing that disorder and impurity in the presence of Śiva,
and everything scattered by the wicked, violent man, / Nandin became full of anxiety: 'What strange thing has happened to me today?
The obstacles mentioned for one devoted to the worship of Śiva / have arrived in this very way due to the adversity of my misfortune.'
Reflecting thus for a long time and washing Śiva's temple, / Nandin returned to his own home by the path he had come.
Then, noticing Nandin looking distracted in mind, the priest / spoke to him these words: 'Why are you distracted in mind?'
Then Nandin addressed the priest with words: / 'Today, O brāhmaṇa, I saw impurity in the presence of Śiva.
By whom this was done there, I do not know at all.' / Then the priest spoke to Nandin thus:
'The one by whom the worship with flowers and the rest was disrupted there, / he is foolish, without doubt, dull-witted regarding what should and should not be done.
Therefore, you should not worry any further, sir. / In the morning, go to that temple of Śiva together with me
in order to watch for the wicked one; I will punish him.' / Hearing these words of that priest,
Nandin stayed at his own home at night with an aching heart. / When that night had passed, he called the priest,
and Nandin went to Śiva's temple together with that noble man. / Having washed [the shrine], he performed worship with various gem decorations
accompanied by the five offerings, together with the brāhmaṇas. / In this manner two watches passed as Nandin praised [the Lord].
Then came that mighty one resembling Kāla, of great strength, / taking the form of Death, exceedingly dreadful, bow in hand, glorious.
Seeing him, Nandin was terrified with fear and hid there; / and the priest likewise suddenly became stricken with fear.
The hunter did what was to be done there just as before, without faltering. / Removing that worship with his foot, he offered bilva leaves.
The hunter worshiped Śiva with meat as the food offering. / Falling like a staff on the ground and rising, he went to his own home.
Seeing that great wonder, Nandin then pondered for a long time / together with the priest, his mind agitated.
The brāhmaṇas were then questioned by him: 'Tell me the truth of the matter.' / Then having deliberated together in accordance with the Dharmaśāstra,
all the brāhmaṇas then spoke to Nandin, who had become fearful: / 'An obstacle to the Lord has arisen, difficult to avert even for the gods.'

"Therefore, bring the liṅga to your own house, best of Vaiśyas."
Thinking "So be it," that Nandī performed a great uprooting of Śiva;

having brought it to his own home and installed it according to the rule,
having made a golden pedestal, splendidly adorned with fresh plantain [leaves],

he worshipped it then with manifold offerings.
Then, on the next day, the hunter came to the shrine of Śiva.

When he looked around, he did not see the liṅga of the Lord.
Abandoning silence, he immediately spoke this with angry cries:

"O Śambhu, where have you gone? Reveal yourself today indeed!
If your sight is not granted, I will abandon this body today!

O Śambhu, O Lord of the world, destroyer of Tripura, Śaṅkara,
O Rudra, O Mahādeva, reveal yourself by yourself!"

Having thus reproached Sadāśiva with sweet words of rebuke,
that resolute hunter, indeed with a knife, his own belly

split open quickly; then, grasping his arm, he spoke aloud in anger:
"O Śambhu, show yourself! Leaving me, where will you go?"
Having thus extracted the entrails [and] pulled out the flesh from everywhere, / the hunter immediately cast [it] into that pit with his hand.

And making his heart pure, he bathed in the Sābhramatī;
likewise, having fetched water and bilva leaves with haste,

having worshipped according to custom, he fell like a rod upon the ground.
When the hunter stood there in meditation near Śiva,

then Rudra appeared, surrounded by the Pramathas,
radiant with the white lustre of camphor, matted-haired, bearing the crescent moon upon his crest.

Taking him by the hand, Rudra said, comforting [him]:
"Hail, hero! O very wise one, you are my devotee, O great-minded one!

Choose a boon, O devotee, whatever is in your mind."
Addressed thus by Rudra, he, Mahākāla, filled with joy,

fell like a rod upon the ground, endowed with supreme devotion.
Then he spoke this to Rudra: "I ask for no boon.

I am your servant, O Rudra; you are my master, there is no doubt.
Grant this, the most praiseworthy [thing] in the world, in birth after birth!

You are mother and you are father, and you are kinsman and friend to me;
you are guru, you are the great mantra; you are ever to be known through the mantras."

Hearing the desireless speech of the hunter, Bhava then
granted him the chief status among attendants and the position of gatekeeper.

Then the three worlds were made to resound with the sound of the ḍamaru,
with the booming roar of kettle-drums, and with the blare of conches.

Then large drums and kettledrums sounded by the thousands.
Hearing that sound, Nandī went quickly out of wonder

to the ascetic grove where Śiva stood surrounded by the Pramathas.
And the hunter was seen then directly by Nandī.

Approaching, that Nandī, filled with wonder, spoke words,
desiring to praise the hunter with supreme absorption:

"Śambhu has been brought here by you; you are a devotee, O scorcher of foes!
I, a devotee of yours, have arrived here; present me unto Śaṅkara!"

Hearing his words, the hunter, filled with haste,
and taking Nandī by the hand, approached Śaṅkara.

Laughing, the blessed Rudra spoke these words to the hunter:
"Tell [me], who is this that you have brought here into the presence of the Gaṇas?"

The hunter said:
"He is your devotee, O God; he is indeed devoted to your worship.
Every day, with gems, rubies, and diverse flowers here,

even with his life and wealth you have been worshipped, without a doubt.
Therefore, receive Nandī, O Lord, who are affectionate to your devotees!"

Mahādeva said:
"I know the fortunate Nandī, who lives by the trade of a Vaiśya.
You are my devotee and my friend, O Mahākāla of great intellect!

Those who are free from worldly pretension and whose minds are guileless,
they are dear [to me], and they are my devotees; they are distinguished, best among men."
Both of them were accepted by Śambhu as his attendants.

Then many aerial chariots of great splendour arrived there;
that best of Vaiśyas was redeemed by that best of hunters of great glory.

They reached the world of Kailāsa by very swift aerial chariots;
they attained indeed the same form as the great-souled Lord.
Both Gaṇas were waved with lights by the daughter of the mountain, like her own sons.

Then the goddess, who walks with the gait of an elephant, laughing, spoke this:
"Just as you are indeed, Mahādeva, so are these two, there is no doubt,

by similarity of form, by gait, and by highly honoured joyous dispositions."
Hearing that speech of the goddess, the hunter and the Vaiśya,

immediately turned their faces away before the eyes of Śaṅkara;
filled with haste, looking at the two Gaṇas of Rudra, they said:

"Both of us are to be shown compassion by you, O three-eyed one;
may we two stand always at your door. Therefore, homage, homage [to you]!"

Knowing their intention, the blessed Bhava, laughing,
spoke with supreme affection: "Let that which you both desire come to be."

From that time forward, these two became the gatekeepers,
standing at the door of Śiva, O goddess, beholding Śiva at midday.

One is Nandī, the other Mahākāla; both these are dear to Śiva.
Those who are sinners or most unrighteous, blind, mute, and lame,

bereft of caste, wicked, outcasts and the like, men of any kind,
having worshipped Dhavaleśvara,

have gone [to his realm] and will go; no doubt should be entertained here.
A bath here, and giving gifts, and proximity to Śaṅkara—

those who have bathed in the Sābhramatī and are worshippers of Dhavaleśvara,
they go to the world of Rudra; no doubt should be entertained here.

Those best of men who perform bathing and giving of gifts here,
having enjoyed the pleasures of righteousness, wealth, and desire, go to the abode of Hara.

And whatever fruit a mortal obtains at an eclipse of the moon or sun, or on the annual day of one's father,
that fruit he will surely obtain.

The wish-yielding cow always comes by all means from heaven;
having arrived, having worshipped that god Śiva in any way,

she goes back toward heaven, O best among the gods, there is no doubt.
By the contact with that milk, the liṅga was made white;

Creatures who die here, O goddess, urged by time,

Situated on the bank of the Sābhramatī is the foremost sacred place among sacred places, / celebrated as Bālāpā, which bestows enjoyment and liberation.

a sacred place upheld by ascetics, the refuge of the gods—
there a maiden performed supreme asceticism, of very firm vows.

A virtuous daughter of the sage Kaṇva, matchless in form upon the earth,
a young woman named Bālāvatī, a virginal celibate student,

she observed the vow of Sāvitrī, endowed with many restraints,
having resolved: 'May Bhāskara be my husband,' O radiant lady.

Ten years passed for her on the bank of the Sābhramatī
as she performed those various vows, extremely difficult to observe, with devotion."

The Lord was pleased by her praise, by her vow, by her austerity and practice of vows, / and by her supreme devotion, an abundance of devotion.

The god of gods, the maker of the day, came to the hermitage; / assuming the form of a brāhmaṇa sage, the high-minded one entered.

Seeing him, supreme through fierce austerity and the best knower of Brahman, / she worshipped that twice-born according to the rule of forest-dwellers.

6.151.m:
She, devoted to the sun and auspicious, said to that ascetic: / 'Lord, tiger among sages, what do you command, O master?

According to my power, I shall give you everything except my own body; / I am a devotee of the sun, and I shall never give my hand [in marriage] to you.

Through vows and observances, and through austerities too, O ascetic, / I must please the sun, the god who is the lord of the three worlds.'

When she had spoken thus, the Sun, as if smiling, gazing upon her / who was firm in her observance, spoke as if consoling [her]:

'You practice fierce austerity, auspicious one, most difficult to perform; / and that for the sake of which your undertaking is, girl, shall indeed be so.

Everything is obtained through austerity; everything rests on austerity; / godhood is attained, gentle one, through austerity, and liberation alone.'

'Receive these five jujube fruits from me, fortunate one.' / Having given the jujube fruits to her, saying, 'Cook [them],' the sun went away.

Without asking that auspicious girl, leaving her behind in the form of a brāhmaṇa, / the highly renowned one stayed not very far away in the village of Indragrāma.

Staying [there] out of a desire to test her disposition, the sun, [disguised as] a brāhmaṇa, / caused a grove of jujube trees to be made, the sun [did so].

6.151.m:
Then that young girl, composed, with folded hands and free from weariness, / placed a fire [on the hearth] to cook the jujube fruits.

The supreme, highly radiant maiden cooked the jujube fruits; / while she was cooking, a very long time passed, O queen of the gods.

A great heap of ashes arose, and the day came to an end; / indeed, a great heap of wood was consumed by the fire.

Having washed her two feet afterwards, in the fire of beautiful sight / she burnt [them] for the sake of the jujube fruits, wishing to please the brāhmaṇa.

Having repeatedly burnt her feet, sinless one, they were held above [the fire]; / then, seeing that action of hers, the god, the maker of the day, was pleased.

Then he revealed his own form to the girl; / highly pleased, he spoke to that girl of very firm vow.

Sūrya said: / 'I am pleased, girl, by your devotion, by your austerity and practice of vows; / therefore let the desired wish of yours, O girl, be fulfilled.

Endowed with austerity, you shall dwell in my home at this holy place; / and this foremost holy place is designated by your name,

known as Bālāpā, situated on the bank of the Sābhramatī, / renowned in the three worlds, praised of old by brāhmaṇa sages.

6.151.m:
A man, having bathed at Bālātīrtha, having stayed three nights, pure, / having seen the face of Raktāditya facing the rising of the sun,

attains the world of Sūrya; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. / On a Sunday, or at an astronomical transit, especially on the seventh lunar day,

at an equinox, at a solstice, and also at an eclipse of the moon or the sun, / having bathed, one should satisfy the gods, the ancestors, and the grandfathers.

Then one should give a cow made of raw sugar, and boiled rice with molasses to brāhmaṇas; / and the worship of Raktāditya with oleander and hibiscus flowers.

Those men who perform [it] indeed dwell in the world of Sūrya; / a man should give a red cow and a single ox that bears the yoke.

He obtains the fruit of a sacrifice, and the man does not go to hell; / one afflicted with disease is freed from illness, one bound is freed from bondage; / by the offering of rice-balls at this holy place, the ancestors attain satisfaction.'

Mahādeva said: / 'Likewise, another great glorification of this holy place, O ascetic, / should be heard, which happened of old and was told by Vyāsa.

Formerly here an old buffalo, worn out by old age, / unable to carry the load, was abandoned by a merchant.

6.151.m:
In the hot season, he went to the great river to drink water; / by fate he sank in the mud, and then fell under the sway of death.

His bones being bathed in the holy water by the power of this sacred place, / he became the king, the son of the lord of Kānyakubja, remembering his previous birth.

Remembering his own story and the great power born of the holy place, / having come and bathed in its water, he gave numerous gifts.

There he established the god of gods, Maheśvara; / having bathed at the holy place here, a man, having worshipped Mahiṣeśvara

and seen the face of Raktāditya, is freed from all sins. / Where the water of the Sābhramatī flows from east to west,

that holy [place] is even greater than Prayāga, bestowing all desires. / What is given to foremost twice-born, what is offered in the fire, the ancestral rite that is performed, the repetition of mantras here becomes imperishable.

A gift of cows, land, sesame, gold, cloth, grain, a bed, a seat, a conveyance, and an umbrella— / whatever desire a human being wishes for, he attains that very desire.

And by the grace of Śrī Maheśa and the power of this holy place, / this Bālāpendra holy place is ever purifying and sin-destroying,

which seeing, all sages become forever free from passion; / where [the holy place] named Māhiṣa, also called Śveta, gives great merit,

having bathed where, O queen of gods, there is no rebirth. / Whatever fruit a man attains when a bath is performed in the Godāvarī,
that fruit, O goddess, he attains at this holy place, without a doubt.'

6.153.m: Mahādeva said: / 'I shall declare another supreme holy place, Durdharṣeśvara, / by the mere remembrance of which even a sinner becomes meritorious.
When the war between gods and demons took place, and the Daityas met their death, / having performed the Durdharṣa vow where the descendant of Bhṛgu,
having worshipped Mahādeva, the unassailable cause of the worlds, / obtained from Tryambaka the lore that revives the dead;
for the sake of the Daityas, Uśanas's holy place became famous on the face of the earth; / having bathed at Kāvyatīrtha and worshipped the god Maheśvara,
known indeed as Durdharṣeśvara, one is freed from all sins. / And the account here should be heard by you, O daughter of the mountain.

Formerly when there was a battle here between Vṛtra and Vāsava, / then the gods were defeated by the Asuras, and Maghavat, the lord of the gods, / having contemplated, 'What is to be done?', went to that guru.
Indra said: / 'You are directly our guru, always the protector of the gods; / you are the foremost of the sages, glorious one; show mercy, O ocean of compassion!
And I have been defeated by Vṛtra; where shall I go, O you of good vows?'
Bṛhaspati said: / 'Listen, lord of gods, I shall tell that by which you will always be happy; / simply carry out my word if you desire your own welfare.
Go then to the Sābhramatī; having gone there, be happy, / where the god named Durdhara, bestowing prosperity, resides constantly;
truly, truly, O lord of gods, he grants desired wishes.' / Having heard the word of the guru, he went towards that river.
Having bathed there, the lord of gods worshipped that Maheśa; / simply from the bathing and worshipping, Śrī Maheśvara was pleased.

Mahādeva said:
Whatever you continually ask for, indeed, I grant all that.
Having heard that speech, the lord of the gods spoke supreme words.

Indra said:
You are the master of all worlds; you alone are the primal cause and supreme state.
Indeed, you, the divine Lord of the Universe, are constantly contemplated by me.

If you are pleased with me, O Lord of the Universe, O Lord of the Gods,
slay Vṛtra, O Mahādeva! This is my great desire.

Mahādeva said:
At your word, O lord of the gods, this Vṛtra has been slain by me.
Take the weapon that is given by me, O lord of the gods.
By it alone, at the proper moment, you will slay him; of this there is no doubt.

Indra said:
Tell me, O Lord of the Universe, what weapon is this by which I shall slay Vṛtra?
Is it greater even than the thunderbolt? When was it fashioned by you?

Mahādeva said:
This Pāśupata weapon was indeed fashioned by me long ago.
It has not been given to anyone, O Śakra; it was kept by me for your sake.

Here bathing has been performed by you, O god, and worship has indeed been done by you.
Therefore, take my weapon, by which you will slay Vṛtra.

And by the grace of the glorious Maheśa, it was then obtained by Maghavan.
With that Pāśupata weapon, Vṛtra of mighty strength was slain.

All that took place here by the grace of the Lord Durdharṣa,
merely from bathing, O goddess of gods, and from worship alone, at that very moment.

6.154.m:
On the bank of the Sābhramatī there is a hidden sacred ford, supremely purifying,
known as Khaṅgadhāra; in the Kali age it will remain hidden.

Where, having bathed by chance or drunk its water at will,
one is freed from all sins and honored in the world of Rudra.

Where the holy Sābhramatī, faithfully following Kaśyapa,
was held by Rudra in his matted hair as she flowed down to the netherworld.

Rudra abides right there under the name Khaṅgadhāra,
where, having bathed, even sinners have gone to heaven, O goddess of gods.

In this very connection, they relate this ancient legendary history:
the supremely difficult observance performed by an outcaste hunter.

Pārvatī said:
What indeed was the name of that outcaste hunter? What observance was undertaken by him?
I wish to hear all of that; please tell it as it truly happened.

Indeed, there is none other in the world best among speakers besides you;
therefore tell me everything, O God, that is pleasing to the one wishing to hear.

Mahādeva said:
Long ago there was an exceedingly terrible, wicked-hearted man named Caṇḍa,
cruel, deceitful, malicious, and a terror to living beings.

Constantly that evil-souled man killed fish with a net;
with iron-tipped lances he killed deer, wild beasts, blackbucks, and porcupines.

Piercing birds of various kinds, he would bring them down,
angrily slaying fowls, and peacocks in particular.

He was an outcaste hunter, very sinful, wicked, fond of wicked people.
His wife was of like kind, unchaste and full of great deceit.

As he roamed about in this manner, much time passed.
Once, at night, the sinner was sitting atop a bilva tree,

holding a bow in his hand and fixing an arrow on the bowstring in order to kill a boar.
Thus the night passed for him, vigilant and without blinking,
in the month of Māgha on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, O daughter of the mountain.

Though filled with anger, he cut down many bilva leaves there,
and they fell upon the liṅga situated at the base of the bilva tree.
And the leaves of the bilva tree—by the stroke of fate, that all became the worship of Śiva.

By him, rinsing his mouth, a great ceremonial bathing [of the liṅga] was performed;
and that was done unwittingly by that evil-minded outcaste.

In the month of Māgha, during the bright fortnight, on the fourteenth day at the rising of the moon,
the outcaste of evil conduct emerged free from sin.

His wife, Pracaṇḍā, came near him,
hopeless and without food, to the place where that outcaste stood.

No boar had been obtained by him, nor deer, nor buffalo;
and for his food, that passionate woman brought rice.

Fierce Pracaṇḍā was seen by him approaching with cruel eyes;
that wife of his fell into the middle of the river's water.

Meanwhile, the wrathful man was addressed by her: 'Come quickly and eat!
Fish and meat have now been brought by me for your sake.

What was done on the previous day, you fool? Meat is not seen by your side!
You have ruined it, you fool, and your family is starving!'

Hearing these words of Caṇḍā, he of terrible form—
by his fast on Śivarātri and by keeping awake through the night—

became purified in inner mind; adhering to a pure observance, he [went] to bathe in the river.
While that evil-souled man was bathing, a dog arrived there.

All the meat was then eaten by the dog, O goddess of gods;
Caṇḍā was enraged and stepped forward to kill that dog.

Then enraged Caṇḍā was restrained by Caṇḍa:
'He should not be killed by you; what wrong has been done by him?'

She said: 'The food has been eaten by this very vile creature!
What will you eat, you fool? You will be hungry today!'

The outcaste said:
'I am well pleased by the fact that the food has been eaten by the dog.
What is the use of this perishable body whose lifespan is exhausted?

Those who nurture the body with all their being, O passionate woman,
those fools are to be known as sinners, cast out of both worlds.

Therefore, abandon pride, desire, and evil-mindedness;
be tranquil by discerning your true being and firm with knowledge of reality.

Today, by the observance of Khaṅgadhāra, I shall cast off this body, O beautiful woman;
what use to me is living for a long time?'
Having spoken thus, drawing a sword, as he was about to sever his own head, / so many Gaṇas arrived, prompted by Śiva.

Many aerial chariots arrived there near him;
and having thus seen those aerial chariots and the attendants,

the outcaste, with supreme devotion, spoke to them:
'Why have all of you arrived, wearing rudrākṣa beads,

all resembling crystal, all crowned with the crescent moon,
with matted locks, clad in hides, adorned with garlands of serpent coils,

endowed with splendor, and possessing prowess equal to Rudra? Tell me fittingly the truth!'
Questioned then by the outcaste, those attendants of Rudra spoke.

The attendants said:
'We have been dispatched, O Caṇḍa, by Śiva, the Supreme Lord.
Come, make haste, and board the aerial chariot together with your wife!

Because of the worship of Śiva's liṅga performed by you during the night,
through the ripening of that act you have attained the supreme state.'

Addressed thus by Vīrabhadra, he spoke as if laughing:
'What merit has been performed by me, a sinful outcaste,

delighting only in hunting, foolish, evil-minded,
and always of sinful conduct? How shall I dwell in heaven?

And how has worship of the liṅga been done today? Let that be told!
Overcome with great wonder, I ask you; kindly tell me!'
Vīrabhadra said: / The god of gods, Mahādeva, named Gaṅgādhara, / the lord of Umā, is pleased today with you and your wife, O Caṇḍa.
Today worship was indeed performed by you incidentally, / while watching for the boar, and bilva leaves
were cut down by you, O Caṇḍa, and fell at that very moment / upon the top of the liṅga; by that you have become virtuous, O lord.
Thus your vigil truly took place atop the great tree; / by that very vigil the Lord of the Universe was pleased.
Under this pretext, O fortunate hunter, by looking for the boar, / the day of Śivarātri was fasted on by you, even if merely by coincidence.
Pleased by that fast and vigil, that great soul, the best of gods, / that exalted granter of boons, grants all boons for your favor.
Thus addressed then by that wise Vīrabhadra, / the Puṣkasa mounted an excellent celestial vehicle as they watched:
all the gaṇas, the gods, and all living beings. / Then kettledrums sounded, and kettle-drums and trumpets in abundance;
lutes, flutes, and mṛdaṅga drums, accompanied by dance and drama. / The lords of the Gandharvas sang, and troops of Apsarases danced.
Fanned with chowries and shaded by various parasols, / with a great festival he was brought into Śiva’s presence.
Even the Puṣkasa then attained [this] through bathing at the sacred ford and worshipping Śiva; / what then of those who, with faith and devotion to Śiva, the Supreme Self,
offer flowers and the like, fruit, incense, betel, and unbroken grains of rice? / Those in this world are Rudras, there is no doubt of this.
Mahādeva said: / Thenceforth that sacred ford became celebrated as Khaṅgadhāra. / In the Kali age, O ruler of the gods, this sacred ford will be hidden.
Those who bathe especially in the month of Māgha, or in Vaiśākha, / or on the full-moon day of Kārttika, are liberated, O delighter of the gaṇas.
Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Bharadvāja, and Gautama / come indeed to bathe and to behold the god who bears the Pināka.
The liṅga is present in three ages, but never in the Kali age, O Pārvatī; / for a curse was pronounced on me then by the sage Viśvāmitra.
Pārvatī said: / Why was a curse pronounced by the sage, O ruler of the gods? / That I wish to hear from you, O god, beyond doubt.
Mahādeva said: / At one time, O goddess, Viśvāmitra of great ascetic heat / came to this most wonderful sacred ford, Khaṅgadhāra.
Having bathed in the Sābhramatī, he gazed upon me; / he stayed there constantly, offering worship in manifold ways.
There some very wicked Kaulika, who wore the form of sin, / placed meat upon Śiva then, O fair lady.
Having seen that meat as well, Viśvāmitra then, however, / spoke there at that time: “A misdeed has been done by a sinner,
yet punishment has not been inflicted on him by Śarva, the Supreme Self. / Therefore, having resolved, I will surely pronounce a curse, beyond doubt.”
Having reflected thus, I was cursed by him then, O goddess:
“In this dreadful Kali age, remain hidden in every way!” / Having thus pronounced the curse, the best of sages departed.
Since that time, O goddess, I am hidden on account of the sage's curse. / If one especially performs worship in my place,
whatever sin they have is destroyed in that very instant. / Those who make an image of me from clay and worship it
especially in this place of mine, certainly dwell in my abode. / In the Kali age it is celebrated by the name Khaṅgadhāreśvara.
In the Kṛta age it is called Mandira; in the Tretā age it is remembered as Gaurava; / in the Dvāpara age it is renowned as Viśva; in the Kali age it is remembered as Khaṅgeśvara.
My abode lies toward the southern part, O ruler of the gods; / knowing this, a wise person who always makes an image right there
and constantly performs worship will attain their desired fruit; / a mortal on earth obtains dharma, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.

Those who offer incense, lamps, food offerings, and sandalwood paste / to the Lord of the World, O ruler of the gods, O great goddess, / will suffer no distress; this is true, truly true, O fair-faced lady.

6.155.m: Mahādeva said: / South of Khaṅgadhāra is a most purifying sacred ford / known as Dugdheśvara, which destroys all sins.
When a man bathes at that sacred ford and beholds Hara as Dugdheśvara, / that person is instantly freed from sorrow born of sin.
Austerity was practiced by Dadhīci on the auspicious bank of the Sābhramatī, / where the Candrabhāgā, immensely meritorious, meets the Gaṅgā.
Bathing, giving, recitation, worship, and austerity there / all attain imperishability through the power of Dugdhatīrtha.
Pārvatī said: / I wish to hear the origin of Dugdheśvara, O lord, / and tell me the greatness of Dugdhatīrtha, O ruler of the gods.
Mahādeva said: / Formerly, in the war between the gods and asuras, the gods were defeated by the Daityas; / taking to flight, they came to the hermitage of Dadhīca.
Leaving their weapons right there, the gods fled in the ten directions. / Later, hearing the clamor arising from the Daityas, Dadhīca,
the descendant of Bhṛgu, drank those weapons after bathing them in water. / In time, all those gods, eager to take back their weapons,
all arrived together with their preceptor, filled with mutual delight. / There snakes were playing with mongooses mutually;
beholding many such wondrous things in that hermitage, / all the gods were filled with the greatest astonishment.
They saw the excellent sage seated upon a seat / where the holy Sābhramatī joins the Candrabhāgā,
shining with supreme splendor like the sun, / a second Fire, together with his wife Suvarcā,
like Brahmā with Sāvitrī; thus that best of sages / was seen by all the excellent gods, who bowed down before him.
The gods, led by Bṛhaspati, then said to him: / “You are already known across the three worlds as a giver,
"And we all have approached you for the sake of begging; / we are all terrified by fear: you should give us the weapons."
Having been spoken to thus, that noble sage of great intellect said to the gods: / "O gods, they have been consumed [by me], having washed [them] with water according to mantra."
Then the gods said to the brāhmaṇa, “For the slaying of the Daityas, / give your bones quickly, O brāhmaṇa!” “They are given,” said the twice-born sage.
Having spoken thus to them, he sent his wife to the hermitage; / then the wise twice-born [sage], delighted, smilingly said to the gods:
“O gods, they were drunk; take them as they are.” / Having said this, O goddess, the twice-born, who knew yoga, resorted to yoga.
Then the gods, smiling, said to the brāhmaṇa with deceptive speech: / “While you are living, O brāhmaṇa, how can we obtain the bones?”
Laughing, the brāhmaṇa sage said: “Stand to one side for a moment; / of my own accord, O gods, I will relinquish my body today.”
"Having spoken thus, O goddess, that twice-born, a knower of yoga, relying on yoga, / immediately went to the world of Brahmā, from which one does not return again."
Then all the gods, seeing that he had attained dissolution, / pondered in their ranks: “How shall we dissect [him]?”
Śacī’s husband summoned Surabhi and said to her: / “Lick the body of the foremost twice-born at my word.”
Agreeing, “So be it,” she licked it that very moment; / and instantly the cow stripped that corpse of flesh.
The gods took up those bones and fashioned weapons; / and from his spine was produced the weapon Brahmaśiras.
Having fashioned arms and missiles, those gods of great strength and prowess / set out in haste, intent on slaying Vṛtra.
Then Suvarcā, the wife of Dadhīca, who had been sent away to ensure the success of the gods’ task, / arrived there and beheld her husband dead, his body dissected.
Learning of all that deed done then by the gods, the virtuous woman grew enraged; / exceedingly furious, Suvarcā, wife of the foremost seer, uttered a curse:
“Ah, all the gods are most wicked, cursed by many, and likewise greedy! / Therefore let all the gods, beginning with Indra, be childless from this day forward!” she spoke.
Having thus cursed those gods, that ascetic woman / sat at the base of a pippal tree, remaining on the bank of the Sābhramatī.
Pregnant, that chaste and virtuous woman tore open her own belly; / and from her womb emerged the fetus of the great-souled Dadhīca.
He was the direct incarnation of Rudra, the great lord Pippalāda; / smiling at his mother's womb, he spoke a momentous word.
Suvarcā [said] to that Pippalāda: “Stay long beside this / pippal tree, O fortunate one, and bring good fortune to all.”
Speaking thus to her son, / that virtuous woman went to her husband through supreme absorption.
Thus Dadhīca's wife attained heaven with her husband. / Those gods, equipped with weapons and missiles, were eager against the Daityas;
the gods headed by Indra arrived, endowed with great strength and prowess. / The wish-granting cow milked where the twice-born attained his end.
Through the power of the sage, the milk turned into the form of a liṅga; / it became known, O goddess, as Dugdheśvara on the bank of the Sābhramatī.
From then on, that sacred bath was celebrated on earth by that name; / incomparable is its glorification, destroying sins upon hearing.
Those men who listen with devotion to the origin of Dugdheśvara / are also freed from sin and go to the supreme realm of Rudra.

6.156.m: Thus ends the one hundred fifty-fifth chapter, named the Glorification of Dugdheśvara, in the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Padma Purāṇa consisting of fifty-five thousand verses.

Mahādeva said: / East of Dugdheśvara lies a supreme, purifying sacred bath, / where the river named Candrabhāgā joins.

Having bathed here, drunk [the water], and performed worship of Śiva, / whatever men assemble here attain religious duties and wealth.

Tīkṣṇāṃśu ('Sharp-rayed'), Mārtaṇḍa, Sūrya, Prabhākara, / Vibhāvasu, Sahasrākṣa ('Thousand-eyed'), and also Pūṣan.

A kṣatriya attains kingship, a vaiśya acquires wealth, / and a śūdra attains devotion; therefore, one should mutter this supreme hymn.

who is manifestly the Vaiṣṇava power, always intent on protecting. / This goddess was installed here on the riverbank by Kṛṣṇa,

who, having conquered the demon Bāṇa in battle, was returning toward Dvārakā. / Through Aniruddha's hymn of praise, she came palpably present.

If a man bathes at that tīrtha with diligence for one year, / seeing the face of Koṭarākṣī, he attains abundant fortune.

Having bathed at the Siddhatīrtha and seen Koṭaravāsinī, / a man is glorified in the world of Rudra by means of a vehicle yoked with lions.

By the mere memory of whom even he was liberated, O fair-faced one! / Therefore, the men who go there share in liberation.

Having gone there and especially performed ablutions, O Pārvatī, / one should then thoughtfully recite the hymn of praise to Koṭarākṣī:

6.158.m:
'Koṭarākṣī, Viśvarūpā, Mahāmāyā, possessing great strength, / Tripurā, slayer of Tripura, Śivā, of the form of Śiva,

the Maiden, called Sārasvatī, Durgā, remover of misfortune, / Bhairavī, Bhairavākṣī, and the goddess Lakṣmī, dear to the people.'

These names have been proclaimed in many ways, O queen of gods. / The best of men who recite them go to the presence of Śiva.

The wise who recite this hymn composed by Aniruddha / are freed from harsh bonds; this is true, truly true, O fair-faced one.

The supreme among tīrthas on earth was made by Koṭarā; / by the mere sight of it, heaps of sins are destroyed.

6.159.m: Mahādeva said: / Greater than this tīrtha is the one renowned as the 'King of Tīrthas'. / Seven rivers flow here, mixed with water [scented with] sandalwood.
Ablution here is distinguished as being a hundred times superior to other tīrthas; / here Vāmana himself, the foremost god among the gods, abides.
Whoever gives an effigy of a cow made of sesame seeds on the twelfth day of the month of Māgha, / freed from all sins, redeems a hundred lineages.
If a restrained man offers even water mixed with sesame seeds to the ancestors here, / he has performed a śrāddha for a thousand years; this is the secret told by the ancestors.
Whoever feeds brāhmaṇas with jaggery and rice pudding at this tīrtha: / when a single brāhmaṇa is fed, a thousand have been fed.

6.160.m: Mahādeva said: / Then one should go to Somatīrtha, hidden on the bank of the Sābhramatī. / Coming out from Pātāla there, Bhava became the fire of time.
A man, having bathed at Somatīrtha and seen Someśvara Śiva, / directly attains the fruit of drinking soma; there is no doubt.
The man becomes handsome, fortunate, an enjoyer, skilled in all scriptures / in this world, and in the next world goes to Śiva.
Regarding this, I shall relate an itihāsa; listen truly, O beautiful one, / hearing which one is freed here from sins such as the murder of a brāhmaṇa.
Extraordinary austerity was practiced by the sage Kauṣītaka: / he went without food, taking pleasure solely in eating dry leaves,
then subsisting on air, devoted to meditation on the self. / In this way, great austerity was performed by him there for many yugas.
At one point, through the working of destiny, Maheśvara was well pleased: / 'Whatever you ask for, O brāhmaṇa, all that I grant.'
Kauṣītaka said: / 'By your favor, O Lord of gods, let a liṅga appear here; / let the god here surely be renowned as Someśvara,
where, having bathed and eaten, one attains one's desired fruit. / If at this site the best of men specially have
the recitation of the Rudra hymn and so forth performed, they attain dharma and artha. / A sonless person attains a son, and an impoverished person attains wealth;
and one desiring a kingdom attains that kingdom—there is no doubt here. / If you are pleased, grant all that to me, O Lord!'
Īśvara said: / Then all was granted to the twice-born by the Lord of gods; / from that time forward that tīrtha became renowned as Somaliṅga.
Those who worship Sadāśiva with sandalwood or with bilva leaves / attain happiness born of sons and other blessings in the human body.
When a Monday arrives, he who goes to the abode of Hara / always attains the desired object through the grace of the Somaliṅga.
Whoever, having gone here, O goddess, offers whatever fruit and the like, / with whatever desire, certainly attains that very thing.
Moreover, those who worship that god, glorious Maheśa, bearer of the Pināka, / with white oleander blossoms and also pārijāta flowers,
they attain the unexcelled realm of Śiva, O best of goddesses.

6.161.m: Mahādeva said: / Then, O goddess, one should go to the Kāpotika tīrtha, / where the ancient water of the Sābhramatī flows.
Whoever offers a piṇḍa there preceded by libations to the ancestors / with wild fruits and flowers on every festive occasion,
and gives an offering to crows and so forth and to dogs and so forth, / that man comfortably crosses over the path of Yama.
Having bathed at that sacred ford on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, a man should worship the god Īśāna, / the supreme Prācīneśvara, with white mustard seeds.
He delivers himself, his ancestors, and his grandfathers, / where a dove, having joyfully offered himself to a guest,
was praised by all the hosts of gods and went to heaven in a celestial chariot. / Since then, that sacred ford has been known as Kāpota.
Tell me, O Lord, how his body was given up by the dove, / and for what reason, O god, lord of gods? I do not know.

Mahādeva said:
At this sacred ford, O goddess, stands an exceedingly great banyan tree; / its branches are indeed endless and are seen spreading widely over the earth.
Creatures live there, as do many birds. / A home was made there by a dove, O ruler of gods.
There dwelt the lord of birds, always devoted to Viṣṇu; / accompanied by his family, he lived securely upon a branch.
On a certain day, O goddess, on the twelfth day—the day of Viṣṇu— / a hawk arrived there as a guest, O fair lady, [saying]:
‘O dove, give me the flesh of your body; / otherwise I will utter a curse!’ So it was said, O daughter of the mountain.
‘Today, on this day of Viṣṇu, I have arrived afflicted with hunger; / therefore that flesh must indeed be given to me, afflicted with hunger, O master!’
Hearing what was said by the hawk, the dove, a great Vaiṣṇava, / then gave his body, O goddess—of this there is no doubt.
By the power of that gift, O best of the gods, there arose the sacred ford— / the great ford Kāpotaka, purifier of purifiers.
A man who bathes at this sacred ford, performs worship of Śiva, / and gives sweet food to guests, O best of the gods,
enjoys happiness in this world and goes to the eternal [realm] of Viṣṇu. / Having given his own body to that great soul,

the dove went to that Vaiṣṇava [abode] as long as the moon and sun endure. / Therefore, going there, O goddess, one should always honor a guest; / when a guest is honored there, one surely obtains everything.

One hundred sixty-fourth chapter.

Thus [ends] the glorious Bhūteśvara Sacred Place. / Higher than this sacred place is the sacred place remembered as Ghaṭeśvara, / where having bathed and having seen him, one surely becomes a sharer in liberation.

Thus [ends] the Ghaṭeśvara Sacred Place. / Then a man should go with devotion to the one renowned as Vaidyanātha; / having bathed at that sacred place, a man intent on the worship of Śiva...

Having bathed there, a man is liberated, O goddess, there is no doubt of this. / I believe it was created on the bank of the Sābharmatī out of a desire for the welfare of people.

Leaving aside all the holy fords that exist on earth, / even those extending up to the ocean, at that truly supreme, wondrous holy ford,

whoever performs a śrāddha there with devotion to Rudra, with senses restrained, / that purified soul attains the fruit arising from all sacrifices.

Whatever is given at Gaṇatīrtha intended for the ancestors, / all of that bears fruit quickly by the grace of the lord of the gaṇas.
